name: Layer 2 Solutions
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Building Upward: How Layer 2 Solutions Scale Without Rewriting the Base Chain
lesson.summary: Layer 2 solutions are systems built on top of a layer 1 blockchain that move most transaction processing off the base chain while still relying on it for final security and settlement, letting a network scale throughput without changing the underlying protocol's own consensus rules.
lesson.body:
Layer 1, covered in the previous chapter, is the base blockchain itself, the network whose own consensus mechanism finalizes transactions. Layer 2, often abbreviated L2, is the general name for a family of systems built on top of a layer 1 that shift most transaction processing off that base chain, using the on-chain versus off-chain distinction from a few chapters back, while still periodically reporting a compact summary or proof back down to layer 1 for final settlement and security.

The efficiency gain comes from asking the base layer to do far less work per user action. Rather than having every layer 1 node individually validate every single transaction, a layer 2 system batches many transactions together off-chain and submits only a small amount of data back to layer 1, perhaps a final account balance, a compressed batch of transaction data, or a cryptographic proof that a batch of transactions was executed correctly. The base chain still ultimately anchors the result, but it never has to individually process each underlying transaction the way it would if all that activity had happened directly on layer 1.

Rollups are the most prominent real world example of this pattern, used by networks including Arbitrum, Optimism, and zkSync, all built on top of Ethereum. Rollups execute transactions off-chain and then post data back to layer 1 along with a mechanism for layer 1 to ultimately act as referee, either a window of time during which anyone can submit fraud proof challenging an incorrect result, an approach called optimistic rollups, or a cryptographic validity proof submitted immediately that mathematically demonstrates the batch was executed correctly, an approach called zk-rollups. Two other layer 2 approaches, state channels and sidechains, take meaningfully different paths to the same general goal and are covered in the next two chapters.

The scaling effect can be substantial. Ethereum's own base layer processes on the order of a few tens of transactions per second, but a rollup built on top of it can bundle thousands of individual user transactions into a single layer 1 posting, giving users of that rollup access to throughput far beyond what interacting with Ethereum's base layer directly would allow, while the rollup's security still ultimately traces back to Ethereum's own consensus mechanism handling the periodic settlement.

None of this is entirely free of new trust assumptions, however. A layer 2 system introduces its own questions, who controls the sequencer that decides the order in which off-chain transactions are processed, how long a dispute or withdrawal window lasts, and whether proofs are actually being verified on layer 1 the way they are supposed to be. Calling something a layer 2 does not automatically mean it carries the same security guarantees as layer 1 itself, that depends entirely on the specific design choices of the system in question, which is exactly why the next few chapters look closely at specific layer 2 architectures rather than treating layer 2 as a single, uniform category.
